'''Rolf William Landauer''' (February 4, 1927 – April 27, 1999) was a [[German American|German-American]] [[physicist]] who made important contributions in diverse areas of the [[thermodynamics]] of information processing, [[condensed matter]] physics, and the conductivity of disordered media.<ref name="Bennett">{{cite book
  | last1 = Bennett
  | first1 = Charles H.
  | first2=Alan B.
  | last2=Fowler
  | chapter = Rolf W. Landauer (1927 - 1999) A biographical memoir
  | title=Biographical Memoirs v. 91 (2009)
  | publisher = [[National Academy of Sciences]]
  | year = 2009
  | isbn = 978-0-309-14560-2
  | doi = 10.17226/12776
  | chapter-url = https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/landauer-rolf.pdf
  }}</ref> Born in Germany, he emigrated to the U.S. in 1938, obtained a Ph.D. in physics from [[Harvard University|Harvard]] in 1950, and then spent most of his career at [[IBM]].

In 1961 he discovered [[Landauer's principle]], that in any logically irreversible operation that manipulates [[information]], such as erasing a bit of memory, [[entropy]] increases and an associated amount of [[energy]] is dissipated as [[heat]].<ref name="Bennett" /> This principle is relevant to [[reversible computing]], [[quantum information]] and [[quantum computing]].  He also is responsible for the [[Landauer formula]] relating the [[electrical resistance]] of a conductor to its scattering properties.  He won the [[Stuart Ballantine Medal]] of the [[Franklin Institute]], the [[Oliver Buckley Prize]] of the [[American Physical Society]] and the [[IEEE Edison Medal]], among many other honors.<ref name="Bennett" />

==Biography==
Landauer was born on February 4, 1927, in [[Stuttgart]], [[Germany]].  He [[emigration|emigrated]] to the United States in 1938 to escape [[Nazi]] persecution of [[Jew]]s, [[graduation|graduated]] in 1943 from [[Stuyvesant High School]], one of [[New York City]]'s mathematics and science [[magnet schools]], and obtained his undergraduate degree from [[Harvard]] in 1945.  Following service in the [[US Navy]] as an [[Electrician's Mate]], he earned his Ph.D. from Harvard in 1950.<ref name=nytobit>{{cite news |author1=George Johnson |title=Rolf Landauer, Pioneer in Computer Theory, Dies at 72 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/04/30/nyregion/rolf-landauer-pioneer-in-computer-theory-dies-at-72.html |url-access=subscription |access-date=21 November 2020 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=30 April 1999 |page=C 21|quote=Rolf W. Landauer, who helped solidify the slippery concept of information and bring it firmly into the mainstream of physics, died on Tuesday at his home in Briarcliff Manor, N.Y. He was 72.}}</ref> His advisor was initially [[Léon Brillouin]] but he finished the thesis under the supervision of [[Wendell H. Furry]].<ref name="Bennett" />

He first worked for two years at [[NASA]], then known as the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, at its [[Glenn Research Center]], then known as the Lewis Research Center, in Cleveland. At the age of 25, he began a career in semiconductors at [[IBM Research]]. As part of the two-man team responsible for managing IBM's Research Division in the mid-1960s, he was involved in a number of programs, including the company's work on semiconductor lasers. In 1969, he was appointed an [[IBM Fellow]].

Much of his research after 1969 related to the kinetics of small structures. He showed that in systems with two or more competing states of local stability, their likelihood depends on noise all along the path connecting them. In electron transport theory, he is particularly associated with the idea, taken from circuit theory, that electric flow can be considered a consequence of current sources as well as applied fields. He was also a pioneer in the area of information handling. His principles have been applied to computers and to the measurement process and are the basis for Landauer's own demonstration that communication, in principle, can be accomplished with arbitrarily little dissipation of energy.<ref>R. Landauer, ‘Minimal Energy Requirements in Communication’, Science 272, 1914 (1996).</ref>

Rolf William Landauer died on 27 April 1999 at his home in [[Briarcliff Manor]] from brain cancer.<ref name=nytobit/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fowler |first1=Alan |author1-link=Alan Fowler (physicist) |last2=Bennett |first2=Charles H. |author2-link=Charles H. Bennett (computer scientist) |last3=Keller |first3=Seymour P. |last4=Imry |first4=Yoseph |author4-link=Yoseph Imry |title=Obituary: Rolf William Landauer |journal=Physics Today |date=October 1999 |volume=52 |issue=10 |pages=104–105 |doi=10.1063/1.882874 |bibcode=1999PhT....52j.104F |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
*Fellow, [[IEEE]]
*Member, [[National Academy of Engineering]]
*Member, [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]]
*Member, [[European Academy of Sciences and Arts]]
*Fellow, [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]
*Honorary doctorate, [[Technion]] in [[Israel]]
*1991 Scott Lecturer at the [[Cavendish Laboratory]] at [[Cambridge University]]
*1992 [[Stuart Ballantine Medal]] of the [[Franklin Institute]]
*Centennial Medal by [[Harvard]] in 1993,
*[[Oliver E. Buckley Prize]] by the [[American Physical Society]] (1995)
*[[LVMH|Moet Hennessey Louis Vuitton]] (LVMH) Science for Art Prize (1997)
*IEEE [[Edison Medal]] (1998) ''For pioneering contributions to the physics of computing and conduction.''
*The Rolf Landauer Medal of the International ETOPIM Association (2009)

The range of his work has been recognized in special issues of two journals, 10 years apart: the ''IBM Journal of Research and Development'' (January 1988) and ''Superlattices and Microstructures'' (March/April 1998).
